evidence: The orchestrator's own `git add -A` at the Batch B commit swept .stamity/review-gate.json into the index and committed it (d5b210b), directly contradicting AD-058 — the decision, filed hours earlier in this same session, that the file stays untracked and un-ignored by design. Caught by reading `git status --porcelain` after the commit and finding it EMPTY where exactly one `??` line was expected. Fixed by `git rm --cached` + amend on the unpushed commit (6477e37); the file is preserved on disk and untracked again.
rationale: the trap is structural and will recur in batches C and D: the file is deliberately neither tracked nor ignored, so `git add -A` and `git add .` both take it, and no gate catches it — the leak gate scans it either way and the suite never reads it. Windows-only signal converted to a universal one.

evidence: The orchestrator's own gate command was UNSOUND: `npm run gate && ... && npm test -- --coverage 2>&1 | tail -N` reports the exit code of `tail`, not of the test run, because bash returns the LAST command in a pipeline unless pipefail is set. Caught at the Batch C integration gate, which printed '[exited with code 0]' while the same output read 'Test Files 1 failed | 168 passed' — a mismatched emissionGoldens snapshot for commands/st-work.md. The earlier Batch A and Batch B gates used the identical shape; both were independently confirmed genuinely green (their output carried a full coverage summary and no failure line, and both were then confirmed by CI on all three legs), so nothing red shipped.
rationale: a green-signal guard that cannot go red is the exact defect class this repo's own history calls out (green-signal guards proved by seeding defects). Remedy applied: gates now run as `set -o pipefail` with output redirected to a file and the exit code echoed explicitly, never piped to tail. Root cause of the masked failure itself: `vitest run -u` given TWO test paths as positional args matched only one file, so the emission golden was never rewritten while the cross-client goldens were.

evidence: Found during the D2 extraction, reported and deliberately NOT changed: init --dry-run and sync --dry-run disagree about the three merged MCP documents. Init predicts created/updated from mere existence (the dry-run leg of writeMcpDocument in src/cli/commands/init/apply.ts); sync's plan lane runs the real merge via planUserMcpJson and can report unchanged, and can additionally surface a shared-name collision via predictMcpMergeRefusal. So `init --force --dry-run` over an already-current tree previews 'updated' where `sync --dry-run` previews 'unchanged', and init's preview can never show the hard-link refusal sync's can.
rationale: a real preview asymmetry in shipped behaviour, not a refactor artifact — a dry run is a promise about what the apply will do, and two verbs answering differently about the same tree is the class of defect this package exists to close. Out of scope for the extraction unit (whose mandate was explicitly refactor-only: any behavioural change is a finding, not an edit). Carried to the review package as an open finding rather than fixed unreviewed at the end of a marathon.

evidence: Both golden suites carry an in-file 'Reviewed refreshes, newest first' ledger whose stated contract is that every snapshot refresh is recorded in BOTH files ('a refresh recorded in only one of them leaves half the emitted surface unaccounted'). The Batch C integration updated 5 crossClientGoldens tree digests and 1 emissionGoldens substitution WITHOUT adding either row — caught at the Batch D integration while reading the convention for the review-gate script refresh. Both closure-run rows now written in both ledgers: the content batch's corpus-prose move (itemised per artifact and per dialect) and the timing-margin pass's single generated script (24741 -> 26669 bytes, manifest hash-only at unchanged byte lengths 16080/54488).
rationale: the ledger is the only artifact that lets a later reader attribute a moved golden line to a named change; a refresh committed without its row converts a reviewed diff into an unexplained one. No gate enforces it — the suites assert the snapshots match, never that the ledger explains them — so it is a convention only a reader catches. Recorded as the second instance this run of a discipline that lives outside the gates (the first: the dogfood sync).
